options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The federal POA rule requires two witnesses, not three.
options.independent_option_analysis: Rule requires two witnesses, not a third state-Board witness.

questions.question_stem: DEA SCHEDULE II POWER OF ATTORNEY: A corporate officer, the designated attorney-in-fact, and two witnesses sign a properly prepared POA using verifiable electronic signatures; no ink signatures appear. No other defect exists. Under 21 CFR 1305.05(f), is the document valid with respect to signature format?
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1305.05(d),(f); 84 FR 51371 (Sept. 30, 2019) (electronic-signature authorization retained after 91 FR 13499 Mar. 20 2026)
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 21 CFR 1305.05(d),(f): each legally required POA signature, including witnesses, may be electronic.

options.option_text: It fails because both witnesses must sign in ink, although the corporate officer may sign electronically.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The federal provision permits electronic signatures by any or all of the persons required to sign.
options.independent_option_analysis: No separate ink-only witness rule is stated in subsection (f).

options.option_text: It can satisfy the signature-format rule; electronic signatures are allowed for the required signatories.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 21 CFR 1305.05(f) explicitly permits electronic execution by any or all required POA signers, including witnesses.
options.independent_option_analysis: Correct: electronic signatures are permitted for all required POA signatories under §1305.05(f).

options.option_text: It is valid only if DEA preapproves every electronic signature as part of the registration application.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A compliant executed POA is retained with order records; individual DEA preapproval is not a requirement of §1305.05(f).
options.independent_option_analysis: The regulation does not require case-by-case advance DEA signature approval.

options.option_text: It fails because any electronic signature converts a paper Form 222 POA into a personal CSOS certificate.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. DEA recognizes electronically signed POAs separately from an individual CSOS signing certificate.
options.independent_option_analysis: A POA executed with e-signatures does not become an individual CSOS certificate.

questions.question_stem: A DEA-registered corporate pharmacy orders Schedule II medicines on DEA Form 222. Its licensed pharmacist manager is not a corporate officer and has never received a POA. A registered-company officer is present. Which federal signer conclusions are supported? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 21 CFR 1305.12(d), as amended Mar. 2026, registrant/authorized corporate officer/POA may sign; 1305.05 POA pathway.

options.option_text: The corporate officer can sign under 21 CFR 1305.12(d) without a separate individual POA if authorized in that capacity.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The 2026 rule permits corporate officers of the registrant to sign Form 222 directly.
options.independent_option_analysis: Qualified corporate officer may sign without receiving a separate POA as a registrant entity officer.

options.option_text: The MOR can sign based only on the title Manager of Record, even without POA or corporate-officer status.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A professional or facility job title alone is not federal Form 222 signature authority.
options.independent_option_analysis: MOR title does not independently confer corporate officer status or DEA Form 222 signing authority.

options.option_text: Every pharmacy technician is an automatic DEA Form 222 signer once hired.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Employment does not create an individual POA or corporate officer status.
options.independent_option_analysis: Neither technician employment nor certification automatically authorizes Form 222 signatures.

options.option_text: The MOR could sign after receiving a valid executed POA meeting 1305.05.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 1305.12(d) also permits an individual with a lawful POA to sign for the registrant.
options.independent_option_analysis: An MOR may become an authorized signer via a valid POA executed under §1305.05.

questions.question_stem: A pharmacy keeps executed DEA Forms 222, but files a technician's properly executed POA only in the individual's private home and refuses to produce it during a DEA inspection. What does 21 CFR 1305.05(a) require?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 21 CFR 1305.05(a) POA kept with relevant executed Forms 222 and inspectable while the covered orders are retained.

options.option_text: The POA must be sent to DEA before each Form 222 is executed.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Federal regulations require retaining the POA with order files, not resubmitting it for each order.
options.independent_option_analysis: POA is kept available for inspection; not submitted to DEA before each order.

options.option_text: It is sufficient to tell DEA the name of the attorney-in-fact by telephone.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. An inspector can require the executed written/electronic POA and its documented validity.
options.independent_option_analysis: Telling DEA a name does not substitute for a retained executed authorization.

options.option_text: A POA may be discarded once the technician has signed the first controlled order.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The POA retention period follows the signed orders and is not exhausted by first use.
options.independent_option_analysis: POA cannot be discarded after the first order if the orders/required retention remain.

options.option_text: Retain the executed POA with relevant order files and make it inspectable.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 1305.05(a) directly requires retention for the same period as orders bearing the attorney's signature and inspection availability.
options.independent_option_analysis: Private off-site filing unavailable during inspection does not meet readily available POA record duty.

questions.question_stem: A pharmacy completes a paper DEA Form 222 with 21 separate Schedule II line items on the same form. All quantities and supplier details are otherwise accurate. What must change?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 21 CFR 1305.12(b): one drug item per numbered line; DEA Form 222 instructions, max 20 line items and additional form if needed.

options.option_text: Keep 21 lines if a second pharmacist signs.
options.original_rationale: Additional signers do not override the form's line-item maximum.
options.independent_option_analysis: Second signer does not create a twenty-first numbered line.

options.option_text: Combine unrelated finished dosage forms into a single item.
options.original_rationale: An order line must describe the same finished or bulk form and quantity; distinct products cannot be hidden under one line.
options.independent_option_analysis: Different finished forms cannot be combined into a single compliant item merely to avoid a second form.

options.option_text: Use an additional DEA Form 222 for the extra item.
options.original_rationale: The current form permits no more than 20 line items; a new form is needed for item 21.
options.independent_option_analysis: Use an additional Form 222 for the 21st distinct item under actual form instructions.

options.option_text: Use the back of Form 222 for unlimited additional items.
options.original_rationale: DEA's prescribed form limits line items instead of permitting an unlimited reverse-side continuation.
options.independent_option_analysis: Unnumbered reverse side or attachment cannot extend numbered-item capacity.

questions.question_stem: The supplier receives a paper Form 222 with an erased drug strength and a handwritten correction. The actual intended order is clear from a telephone call. Which action is authorized?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 21 CFR 1305.15(a),(b),(d): altered/erased paper Form 222 unfillable and requires a new Form 222; preserve rejection.

options.option_text: Ship the product after marking the correction with the supplier's initials.
options.original_rationale: A defective paper order cannot be repaired by the supplier.
options.independent_option_analysis: Supplier initials cannot cure an altered order for filling.

options.option_text: Return the defective order and request a properly completed new Form 222.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1305.15 expressly bars filling altered orders and bars correction of the defective form.
options.independent_option_analysis: Supplier returns defective form with reason and purchaser issues a new properly executed form.

options.option_text: Have the purchaser telephone the quantity to create an emergency Form 222.
options.original_rationale: An informal call is not the required replacement controlled-substance order.
options.independent_option_analysis: Oral quantity amendment does not create a replacement Form 222.

options.option_text: Supply a smaller quantity from the altered order.
options.original_rationale: A defective Form 222 cannot be partially filled merely because a smaller amount is requested.
options.independent_option_analysis: Sending a smaller quantity does not permit filling altered defective order.

questions.question_stem: Supplier S cannot fill a Schedule II order and properly endorses its untouched DEA Form 222 to Supplier T. Which distribution scenario is allowed under the endorsement rule?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 21 CFR 1305.14(a)-(b): originally named supplier endorses unfilled order to second supplier, who supplies direct to purchaser; first supplier cannot partly fill endorsed form.

options.option_text: Supplier T fills it alone and ships to the original purchaser.
options.original_rationale: After endorsement, the first supplier may not fill any part; the second supplier may fill and ship directly to purchaser.
options.independent_option_analysis: Properly endorsed order may be filled by second supplier alone and sent directly to original purchaser.

options.option_text: S fills half while T fills the rest.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1305.14 prohibits the first supplier from fulfilling any part after endorsement.
options.independent_option_analysis: Original supplier cannot fill part of the endorsed order.

options.option_text: T ships the containers to S for repackaging before delivery.
options.original_rationale: The endorsed-order provisions require shipment directly to the original purchaser.
options.independent_option_analysis: Second supplier must ship directly to original purchaser, not return for first supplier repackaging.

options.option_text: The purchaser endorses the form after S declines.
options.original_rationale: Only the supplier to whom the original Form 222 was made out may endorse it.
options.independent_option_analysis: Purchaser does not endorse a Form 222 to alternate supplier; first supplier has endorsement authority.

questions.question_stem: A registered distributor's CSOS software detects that the DEA digital certificate used to SIGN a Schedule II electronic order had already expired before signature. Which response follows the federal rule?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 21 CFR 1305.25(a)(3),(b)-(d): expired/revoked certificate at signature invalid; cannot repair; purchaser must issue new CSOS order.

options.option_text: Accept because the receiving pharmacy is a current DEA registrant.
options.original_rationale: Current pharmacy registration does not validate an order signed with an expired certificate.
options.independent_option_analysis: Current registration cannot cure a digital certificate expired before order signature.

options.option_text: Have the supplier edit the certificate timestamp and reprocess.
options.original_rationale: Neither party may correct a defective electronic order.
options.independent_option_analysis: Editing certificate/timestamp is impermissible defective-order correction.

options.option_text: Print the invalid electronic order and treat it as a signed paper Form 222.
options.original_rationale: A printout does not cure a failed digitally signed order.
options.independent_option_analysis: Printing an invalid electronic order does not convert it to signed DEA paper Form 222.

options.option_text: Reject the order and have the purchaser submit a new valid electronic order.
options.original_rationale: Expired-before-signature certificates disqualify the order under 21 CFR 1305.25.
options.independent_option_analysis: Reject, give nonacceptance reason, and require new valid electronically signed order.

questions.question_stem: DEA issues a final rule controlling an existing, formerly nonscheduled medicine effective December 1. A pharmacy already stocks it. Which federal controlled inventory step is due on the effective date?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 21 CFR 1304.11(d): newly scheduled drug stock inventory on scheduling rule's effective date.

options.option_text: Record it for the first time only at the pharmacy's next ordinary biennial inventory.
options.original_rationale: Newly scheduled substances have a special inventory timing rule in addition to ordinary biennial inventories.
options.independent_option_analysis: Effective-date inventory is independent of the next regular biennial inventory.

options.option_text: Inventory the on-hand substance as of its effective scheduling date.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1304.11(d) requires an inventory on the effective date when a previously uncontrolled substance becomes scheduled.
options.independent_option_analysis: On-hand newly federally scheduled substance must be inventoried on effective date.

options.option_text: Dispose of all on-hand product instead of inventorying it.
options.original_rationale: DEA scheduling does not by itself mandate discarding otherwise lawful stock.
options.independent_option_analysis: No general duty to dispose instead of inventory.

options.option_text: Count only packages received after the new scheduling order becomes effective.
options.original_rationale: The on-hand inventory includes preexisting stock newly subject to control.
options.independent_option_analysis: Newly scheduled stock possessed before effective date must be included, not just later deliveries.

questions.question_stem: A DEA-registered pharmacy keeps Schedule II acquisition records intermixed with Schedule III–V files and says any electronically searchable index eliminates all separation requirements. Which federal record system is required?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 21 CFR 1304.04(h)(1)-(3): Schedule II inventories/records separate; Schedule III–V separate or readily retrievable.

options.option_text: One unsorted folder for every controlled schedule is sufficient if the pharmacy's finance manager can eventually locate an invoice.
options.original_rationale: Schedule II records must be kept separate rather than merely retrievable with effort.
options.independent_option_analysis: An unsorted combined record file does not satisfy Schedule II segregation.

options.option_text: All Schedule III–V records must be filed separately from one another, with their own DEA facility registration.
options.original_rationale: For Schedule III–V, separate storage or readily retrievable records suffice; individual separate registrations are not required.
options.independent_option_analysis: Schedule III–V records need not each be in isolated files or registrations.

options.option_text: Separate Schedule II records from other records; keep Schedule III–V records separate or readily retrievable.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1304.04(h) distinguishes strict Schedule II separation from the Schedule III–V alternative.
options.independent_option_analysis: Schedule II records separate from all others, SIII–V separate or readily retrievable: correct.

options.option_text: Dispose of invoices after the computerized purchasing balance is reconciled.
options.original_rationale: DEA acquisition and inventory records must be retained under federal and applicable state rules.
options.independent_option_analysis: An electronic reconciliation does not extinguish record-retention rules.

questions.question_stem: At the federal biennial inventory, the pharmacy has a partially filled Schedule IV bottle originally containing 1,500 tablets and a partially filled Schedule II bottle originally containing 100 tablets. Which counting rule applies?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(6)(i)-(ii): exact count for SII; exact SIII–V only when opened container currently holds >1000 tablets/capsules. The scenario only gives original 1,500-tablet package, NOT current remaining count.
questions.scope_or_source_caveat: MATERIAL STATED-FACT DEFECT. Change stem to specify actual remaining Schedule IV count (for instance 1,200 tablets, explicitly on hand now) and version/review scoring history, or WITHDRAW this item from readiness tests. Do not score the existing question as validated.

options.option_text: Estimate the remaining count in both.
options.original_rationale: Schedule II quantities require an exact count.
options.independent_option_analysis: False: Schedule II opened container requires exact physical count.

options.option_text: Estimate Schedule IV because it is not Schedule II, and count Schedule II exactly.
options.original_rationale: A Schedule III–V container holding more than 1,000 tablets or capsules requires an exact count.
options.independent_option_analysis: Potentially permissible to estimate Schedule IV if current remaining count ≤1000, so this distractor could also be valid. Stem is missing current count.

options.option_text: Exact-count both the Schedule II and the over-1,000-tablet Schedule IV bottles.
options.original_rationale: Schedule II always requires an exact count; the >1,000 tablet Schedule IV container also does.
options.independent_option_analysis: As keyed C, exact-count Schedule IV is required only if current contents >1000. Original bottle size 1500 does NOT prove that condition; ambiguous key.

options.option_text: Count only unopened bottles.
options.original_rationale: The inventory must include all controlled substances on hand, including opened containers.
options.independent_option_analysis: Unopened-only inventory ignores opened controlled stock.

questions.question_stem: A newly registered retail pharmacy opens for business on Monday with zero federally controlled substances physically present or under its control. Its first Schedule III shipment will arrive Friday. What initial DEA inventory entry is required?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 21 CFR 1304.11(b),(c): record an initial zero inventory if business commences without controlled substances; subsequent receipts separately recorded.

options.option_text: Record a zero initial inventory on opening day, then track later receipts.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1304.11(b) requires an initial inventory on first engaging in registered activity, including an affirmative zero record.
options.independent_option_analysis: Record zero controlled stock on first business day as initial inventory when none on hand.

options.option_text: Delay the initial inventory until Friday when stock arrives.
options.original_rationale: A zero-stock first-business-day inventory is still required.
options.independent_option_analysis: First shipment does not defer zero initial inventory.

options.option_text: Mark all future stock as on hand on Monday.
options.original_rationale: An inventory must reflect actual controlled substances on hand at the specified time.
options.independent_option_analysis: Future receipts must not be represented as already on hand at opening.

options.option_text: Wait two years for the first inventory because no controlled product was stocked at opening.
options.original_rationale: The biennial inventory follows, rather than replaces, the initial inventory.
options.independent_option_analysis: Biennial inventory follows initial inventory; not a replacement.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts resident retail pharmacy CONFIRMS an employee stole one tablet of a Schedule IV medication this afternoon. The pharmacist asks whether the small quantity eliminates Board reporting. Which action is required?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: MA Board Policy 2026-01 §§II(A) and 247 CMR 20.03(7): every confirmed theft/pilferage/diversion regardless of schedule/quantity must be reported within 7 calendar days.

options.option_text: Omit reporting because one tablet cannot be significant.
options.original_rationale: Board Policy 2026-01 covers ALL confirmed employee pilferage regardless of amount.
options.independent_option_analysis: Confirmed theft of one Schedule IV tablet is reportable under specific any-theft rule.

options.option_text: Report to the Board only if the medication is Schedule II.
options.original_rationale: The confirmed theft category includes every controlled schedule.
options.independent_option_analysis: Loss reporting is not confined to Schedule II.

options.option_text: Wait for a criminal conviction before filing.
options.original_rationale: The policy addresses confirmed theft/diversion rather than a final criminal conviction.
options.independent_option_analysis: No criminal conviction is required before reporting confirmed loss/theft.

options.option_text: File the confirmed theft report with the Board within seven days.
options.original_rationale: The Board's deadline and report apply to any confirmed theft; federal obligations are independent.
options.independent_option_analysis: Confirmed theft triggers Board report within seven calendar days; other DEA/DPH duties analyzed separately.

questions.question_stem: A pharmacy detects a two-tablet Schedule II perpetual-inventory discrepancy. A documented receiving error is plausible, so it has not determined whether a true loss or theft occurred. What is the safest legally supported next step?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: MA Board Policy 2026-01: do not report unconfirmed losses to Board; investigate, document insignificant adjustments/possible errors. 247 CMR 9.21(8)(c)-(d) requires MOR investigation/reconciliation.
questions.scope_or_source_caveat: Applies to a resident community pharmacy with a discrepancy that is not yet confirmed theft/loss. Separate DPH health-facility reporting for suspected events may differ.

options.option_text: Automatically report two tablets as confirmed employee diversion without investigating.
options.original_rationale: The initial discrepancy is not proof of a particular cause or a confirmed theft.
options.independent_option_analysis: A discrepancy cannot automatically be labeled confirmed diversion; investigate first.

options.option_text: Investigate the stock discrepancy promptly, then determine which reports apply.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 9.21 requires MOR investigation, while federal significant-loss and Board confirmed-loss thresholds must be assessed.
options.independent_option_analysis: Promptly investigate discrepancy, preserve inventory evidence, determine which reports apply: correct.

options.option_text: Erase the discrepancy and restart the inventory without documentation.
options.original_rationale: Editing away unexplained quantities defeats the reconciliation requirement.
options.independent_option_analysis: Deleting or resetting discrepancy loses controlled substance accountability.

options.option_text: Ignore the issue unless the next biennial count also differs.
options.original_rationale: MA requires ongoing reconciliation and investigation rather than biennial deferral.
options.independent_option_analysis: Do not postpone investigation to the next biennial count; MA SII reconciliation also every 10 days.

questions.question_stem: A licensed Massachusetts hospital pharmacy's nursing unit notices a likely missing Schedule II dose; hospital investigation is underway and theft is suspected but not yet proven. What reporting rule applies to this health-care facility?
questions.author_citation: 105 CMR 700.005; MA DPH General Accountability Guidelines, Thefts or Losses
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: MA DPH hospital/clinic accountability guidance and DPH DCP reporting: theft or loss whether suspected or confirmed must be reported immediately; 105 CMR 700.005 controls.
questions.scope_or_source_caveat: DPH hospital/clinic guidance distinguishes suspected hospital loss from Board resident pharmacy Policy 2026-01 confirmed-loss reporting. DPH written DIR follow-up requirements apply separately.

options.option_text: Apply only the community-pharmacy Board RLCS procedure and defer all other communication.
options.original_rationale: The facility-specific DCP guidelines impose distinct reporting duties.
options.independent_option_analysis: Hospital suspected missing controlled stock cannot be managed solely by Board RLCS and deferred DPH contact.

options.option_text: Submit DEA Form 106 and ignore Massachusetts reporting until the investigation is finished.
options.original_rationale: Federal forms do not displace the health-care facility's immediate state notification.
options.independent_option_analysis: Federal Form 106 alone cannot replace immediate DPH notice in state-regulated facility.

options.option_text: Notify the DPH Drug Control Program immediately about the suspected loss.
options.original_rationale: The state's hospital/clinic accountability guidance requires immediate DCP reporting of suspected or confirmed theft/loss.
options.independent_option_analysis: Immediately report suspected loss to DPH Drug Control Program, even while investigating.

options.option_text: Wait for the next weekly nursing-unit audit before informing anyone.
options.original_rationale: Weekly QA reviews do not defer immediate suspected-theft/loss reporting.
options.independent_option_analysis: Weekly unit audit does not replace immediate DPH notification.

questions.question_stem: A DEA-registered Massachusetts retail pharmacy confirms a reportable Schedule II theft on Monday, November 2, 2026. There are no holidays. Which timing statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 21 CFR 1301.76(b) initial notice 1 business day and Form 106 45 days; MA Board Policy 2026-01 RLCS/Form106 if applicable within 7 calendar days

options.option_text: The federal initial written DEA field-division notice is due within one business day of discovery.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1301.76(b) specifies one business day for initial federal notice.
options.independent_option_analysis: Federal initial theft notice is within 1 business day.

options.option_text: The Massachusetts Board RLCS report must be submitted within one business day.
options.original_rationale: The Board Policy 2026-01 deadline is seven calendar days, not the DEA initial-notice clock.
options.independent_option_analysis: MA RLCS duty is 7 calendar days, not DEA initial-notice clock.

options.option_text: The DEA Form 106 must be filed within 45 days of discovery through the federal secure network.
options.original_rationale: This separate 45-day federal Form 106 deadline appears in 21 CFR 1301.76(b).
options.independent_option_analysis: Federal Form 106 completion deadline 45 days after discovery; MA may require earlier copy.

options.option_text: The resident pharmacy must submit the Board RLCS and Form 106 if applicable within seven calendar days of the confirmed event.
options.original_rationale: Board Policy 2026-01 has its own seven-calendar-day reporting process.
options.independent_option_analysis: MA resident pharmacy reports RLCS and applicable Form 106 within seven calendar days.

questions.question_stem: At a DEA-authorized collection receptacle in a registered Massachusetts pharmacy, an ultimate user arrives with their lawfully held Schedule II tablets. They offer the closed bottle to a pharmacy technician to count before putting it in the receptacle. What is required?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 21 CFR 1317.75(b)-(c): ultimate user personally deposits lawfully held SII–V directly; collector personnel do not individually take/count it.

options.option_text: Technician counts every tablet, writes a return prescription entry, then deposits them.
options.original_rationale: Collector staff may not individually handle, count, or inventory the ultimate-user drugs after collection; the user deposits them.
options.independent_option_analysis: Technician cannot receive for personal counting/inventory entry before deposit.

options.option_text: Have the ultimate user place the drugs directly in the collection receptacle, without staff handling.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1317.75(c) forbids transferring collected substances to another person and prohibits postdeposit individual handling.
options.independent_option_analysis: Have ultimate user directly deposit, with no intermediary staff handling.

options.option_text: Place the product in the pharmacy's own expired Schedule II inventory.
options.original_rationale: Ultimate-user property entering an authorized collection is not pharmacy-owned saleable stock.
options.independent_option_analysis: Ultimate-user take-back is not pharmacy's own expired controlled stock.

options.option_text: Return controlled drugs to the patient because collectors may accept only noncontrolled drugs.
options.original_rationale: Authorized collectors may take lawfully held ultimate-user Schedule II–V medications.
options.independent_option_analysis: Schedule II–V lawfully held by ultimate user may be deposited; collection is not restricted to noncontrolled.

questions.question_stem: At a DEA-authorized pharmacy collection receptacle, a filled removable inner liner is removed by two collector employees. One wants to unseal and sort the tablets before shipping the liner for destruction. Which procedure complies?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 21 CFR 1317.60(a)-(c) inner liner immediately sealed by 2 employees and not reopened; 1317.75(g) two employee supervision on liner removal.

options.option_text: Seal the liner after removal using two employees; do not reopen it or sort the contents.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1317.60(c) requires immediate two-employee sealing and forbids reopening, x-raying or analyzing the sealed liner.
options.independent_option_analysis: Two employees seal removed liner immediately and never reopen: correct.

options.option_text: Sort pills to determine whether a Schedule II Form 222 is needed for the returned patient tablets.
options.original_rationale: After collection the liner's contents may not be sorted and patient take-back does not create an ordinary purchase order.
options.independent_option_analysis: Returned drugs are not individual order form transactions to sort.

options.option_text: Store the unsealed inner liner in an office desk until the next business day.
options.original_rationale: The regulation requires sealing immediately upon removal.
options.independent_option_analysis: Unsealed liner office-desk storage violates prompt sealing and chain of custody.

options.option_text: Combine the liner with the pharmacy's defective inventory and treat it as an ordinary purchase return.
options.original_rationale: A collected ultimate-user liner is not the registrant's pharmacy inventory.
options.independent_option_analysis: Collector liner is not mixed with registrant's own expired pharmacy stock.

questions.question_stem: A registered pharmacy lawfully destroys its own expired Schedule III stock on-site using an approved method and two authorized employee witnesses. Which statements describe the federal destruction record? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 21 CFR 1317.95(d), 1304.21(e) and DEA Form 41 instructions: two employee witnesses, retained destruction record at least 2y; routine DEA submission not required.
questions.scope_or_source_caveat: Includes DEA Form 41 guidance, which supports the section-specific reporting/retention implementation; destruction method must meet §1317.90 and any MA rules.

options.option_text: Form 41 is never needed because the substance is Schedule III rather than II.
options.original_rationale: Registrant destruction recordkeeping extends beyond Schedule II.
options.independent_option_analysis: Schedule III owned expired product destroyed on-site still requires appropriate Form 41 destruction record.

options.option_text: The two authorized witnesses document that they observed the destruction.
options.original_rationale: DEA's Form 41 witness certification requires the signatures of two authorized employees.
options.independent_option_analysis: Two employee witnesses must actually observe and sign destroyed-substance record.

options.option_text: Send the Form 41 to DEA automatically after every destruction, without exception.
options.original_rationale: The current DEA Form 41 instructions say retention is generally required, submission only on request.
options.independent_option_analysis: Form 41 need not routinely be submitted to DEA unless requested.

options.option_text: Retain the destruction record for at least two years and make it available to DEA upon request.
options.original_rationale: The DEA Form 41 instructions apply the federal at-least-two-year record retention requirement.
options.independent_option_analysis: Keep destruction record at least 2 years and make available on request.

questions.question_stem: A registered pharmacy moves its DEA-authorized collection receptacle next to an unattended front entrance so customers may deposit Schedule II medicine after the pharmacy closes. Which action is supported by 21 CFR 1317.75?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 21 CFR 1317.75(d)-(f): collection receptacle near monitored pharmacy staff; opening inaccessible when employee absent (except NTP-specific framework).

options.option_text: Allow the receptacle to remain open after hours if it is permanently bolted down.
options.original_rationale: Permanent fastening does not eliminate staffed monitoring and closure controls.
options.independent_option_analysis: Permanent bolting does not permit unsupervised after-hours access.

options.option_text: Allow the store security guard to open the liner at closing to inventory deposited pills.
options.original_rationale: The collector liner cannot be opened for sorting or inspection.
options.independent_option_analysis: Security guard cannot open inner liner to inventory contents.

options.option_text: Keep the collection receptacle monitored and closed when staff are absent.
options.original_rationale: The regulation requires supervised location and limits access during periods without employee monitoring.
options.independent_option_analysis: Monitor and lock/make opening inaccessible when employees absent: correct.

options.option_text: Accept all Schedule I–VI controlled substances since the receptacle has an inner liner.
options.original_rationale: The federal collection receptacle authorization is limited to lawfully held Schedule II–V drugs and permitted noncontrolled substances.
options.independent_option_analysis: Authorized receptacles may collect SII–V plus noncontrolled if applicable, not S I/VI 'controlled substances'.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts-licensed NONRESIDENT pharmacy is selected for a Board inspection. The facility offers records but says the Commonwealth must pay all costs because the operation is physically outside Massachusetts. Under 247 CMR 9.24, who pays?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 247 CMR 9.24(1)-(3): all Board inspection costs for licensed nonresident pharmacy borne by nonresident pharmacy/applicant.

options.option_text: The state pays every inspection expense, even when investigating a licensed nonresident applicant.
options.original_rationale: The rule specifically allocates nonresident inspection expenses to the applicant or pharmacy.
options.independent_option_analysis: Commonwealth does not automatically bear nonresident inspection expenses.

options.option_text: The nonresident pharmacy or applicant bears all costs of the Board inspection.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 9.24(2) expressly assigns these costs to the nonresident licensee/applicant.
options.independent_option_analysis: Board rule expressly assigns all nonresident inspection costs to nonresident applicant/licensee.

options.option_text: The nearest Massachusetts retail competitor pays the costs because it serves the same patients.
options.original_rationale: Another unrelated pharmacy is not assigned the facility's regulatory inspection expenses.
options.independent_option_analysis: Competing pharmacy is not liable for regulated facility inspection.

options.option_text: Only DEA may inspect an out-of-state facility, so the Board cannot inspect any records.
options.original_rationale: Massachusetts oversight of its nonresident licensee is not displaced by federal DEA authority.
options.independent_option_analysis: Massachusetts Board may inspect regulated nonresident pharmacy; DEA is not sole oversight.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy responds to a two-violation Board inspection with one sentence: 'All problems fixed.' Which required correction-plan elements are missing? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 247 CMR 9.25(1)-(4): written, violation-specific corrective plan contents

options.option_text: A separate corrective action for each cited violation.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 9.25(2) requires violation-specific plans.
options.independent_option_analysis: Correction for each violation required.

options.option_text: Expected completion or implementation dates.
options.original_rationale: The written plan must state expected dates.
options.independent_option_analysis: Dates/timeline for implementation required.

options.option_text: Identification of responsible individuals and required MOR/supervisor signatures.
options.original_rationale: The rule requires individuals responsible and relevant signatories.
options.independent_option_analysis: Identified responsible individuals and applicable signatures required.

options.option_text: A mandatory FDA preapproval letter for every cited Board violation.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 9.25 does not make FDA approval a universal plan element.
options.independent_option_analysis: FDA prior approval for every Board violation is not required.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy keeps electronic Schedule III–V prescription records on a contracted cloud server. DEA requests inspection and a readable export at the registered pharmacy. What response is required?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 21 CFR 1304.04(a),(h)(5): eRx controlled records may be held remotely but readable, sortable, printable or transferred at registered location.

options.option_text: Refuse because electronically stored prescriptions may be inspected only at the cloud provider's headquarters.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1304.04(h)(5) requires ready retrieval at the pharmacy's registered location.
options.independent_option_analysis: Cloud server location does not bar inspection at registered pharmacy.

options.option_text: Print a monthly aggregate total with no patient, drug, prescriber or fill information.
options.original_rationale: A summary lacking the required prescription-level fields is not sufficient.
options.independent_option_analysis: Aggregate totals cannot substitute for patient/prescriber/drug/date prescription-level data.

options.option_text: Produce readable, sortable electronic prescription records at the registered location for inspection.
options.original_rationale: The e-prescription application must support prompt inspection, printing or transfer and sorting by required fields.
options.independent_option_analysis: Readable sortable eRx records readily retrievable at pharmacy must be furnished.

options.option_text: Destroy electronic records after 30 days when the patient receives the medication.
options.original_rationale: Federal records have an at-least-two-year period and applicable state rules may be longer.
options.independent_option_analysis: At least two-year federal retention, not destruction after 30 days.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy's security video showing routine stock activity is 20 days old. Separate footage covers a suspected controlled-substance theft from 11 months ago. Which retention rule is correctly stated?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 247 CMR 9.21(4): at least 14 days surveillance generally, at least two years for known or suspected theft/diversion.

options.option_text: Every video must be destroyed after exactly 14 days.
options.original_rationale: Fourteen days is a general minimum, not a mandatory deletion date; theft footage has a longer rule.
options.independent_option_analysis: Fourteen days is a minimum, not a mandatory deletion date.

options.option_text: Keep all surveillance video forever.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 9.21 specifies minimum periods rather than perpetual retention.
options.independent_option_analysis: There is no categorical lifetime retention duty for every video.

options.option_text: Delete suspected-theft footage after 14 days if no police report was made.
options.original_rationale: Known or suspected theft/diversion triggers a two-year minimum retention.
options.independent_option_analysis: Suspected theft footage has two-year minimum, even without police report.

options.option_text: Keep suspected-theft video two years and routine recordings at least 14 days.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 9.21(4) differentiates routine and known/suspected diversion video records.
options.independent_option_analysis: Keep theft footage 2 years and routine recordings at least 14 days.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy receives an FDA Warning Letter identifying unlawful drug-quality practices. The owner forwards it to the company's legal department but not to the Board. When must the pharmacy supply the Board a copy?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 247 CMR 20.03(6): pharmacy must provide Board copy of FDA warning letter/agency inspection or investigation report within 14 calendar days of receipt.

options.option_text: Only when the FDA files a criminal charge.
options.original_rationale: A criminal filing is not a prerequisite to the state reporting rule.
options.independent_option_analysis: Criminal filing is unnecessary; warning-letter receipt triggers independent duty.

options.option_text: Only if the pharmacy chooses to publish it in its annual CQI report.
options.original_rationale: An annual CQI report is not the required notice.
options.independent_option_analysis: Annual CQI is not a substitute for Board agency-copy submission.

options.option_text: Within 14 calendar days of receiving the FDA letter.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 20.03(6) covers FDA warning letters and inspection/investigation reports received from agencies.
options.independent_option_analysis: Copy of covered FDA Warning Letter due within 14 calendar days of receipt.

options.option_text: After the pharmacy completes all corrections, regardless of the date.
options.original_rationale: Corrective actions do not replace the 14-day copy deadline.
options.independent_option_analysis: Corrective actions do not toll reporting deadline.

questions.question_stem: Two Massachusetts licensed compounding facilities learn that products they previously dispensed into Massachusetts were defective. X is a sterile CSP, Y is a complex nonsterile compounded preparation. Which reporting statements apply? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 247 CMR 20.06(2),(3): report defective sterile and complex nonsterile compounded preparations within 7 days of identification.

options.option_text: X's qualifying facility must report the defective sterile preparation within seven days after identifying it.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 20.06(2) sets this deadline.
options.independent_option_analysis: Sterile facility reports defective CSP within 7 days of identification.

options.option_text: Neither event must be reported unless a patient is hospitalized.
options.original_rationale: The defect-reporting duty does not depend on an actual serious injury.
options.independent_option_analysis: Serious injury/hospitalization is not a precondition for defective compounding report.

options.option_text: Y's qualifying facility must report the defective complex-nonsterile preparation within seven days of identification.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 20.06(3) separately addresses complex nonsterile products.
options.independent_option_analysis: Complex nonsterile facility has parallel 7-day defective compound report.

options.option_text: Both may defer reporting until the next annual compounding-volume submission.
options.original_rationale: Annual volume reports do not postpone a seven-day defective-product notice.
options.independent_option_analysis: Annual compounding volume filing is independent from 7-day defect notice.

questions.question_stem: A pharmacist Manager of Record submitted a report to the Massachusetts Board about improper dispensing that caused death. Staff propose deleting the associated incident records three years after filing because the CQI program is complete. What is the minimum retention under the specific reporting rule?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 247 CMR 20.02(4): records of improper dispensing causing serious injury/death/serious drug events retained at least 5 years from filing report.

options.option_text: Only until the next monthly CQI meeting.
options.original_rationale: Reporting records carry a separate minimum retention period.
options.independent_option_analysis: Monthly CQI meeting does not end retention.

options.option_text: Keep the report-related records five years after filing with the Board.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 20.02(4) expressly requires a minimum five years from report filing.
options.independent_option_analysis: Five years from Board filing is the express minimum.

options.option_text: Exactly two years from the original prescription date.
options.original_rationale: The two-year rule is not the specific five-year serious-event reporting retention.
options.independent_option_analysis: Two years from Rx date is not this serious-event reporting record clock.

options.option_text: No retention requirement exists once the Board acknowledges receipt.
options.original_rationale: Acknowledgment does not remove the stated five-year duty.
options.independent_option_analysis: Board acknowledgement does not extinguish five-year retention.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts-licensed nonresident pharmacy's designated Massachusetts-licensed pharmacist in charge (PIC) resigns on June 1, 2026. Management assumes the 90-day application period eliminates any earlier Board notice. What does 247 CMR 20.05 require?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 247 CMR 20.05(2): nonresident MA-licensed designated PIC resignation/termination/change notice within 14 calendar days.

options.option_text: No notice because the pharmacy is outside Massachusetts.
options.original_rationale: Nonresident pharmacies have a designated Massachusetts-licensed PIC reporting duty.
options.independent_option_analysis: Nonresident status does not exempt PIC notice.

options.option_text: Notify the Board of the nonresident PIC change within 14 days.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 20.05(2) separately requires timely notice, even where licensing applications have other deadlines.
options.independent_option_analysis: Notice within 14 calendar days; longer application deadlines do not postpone it.

options.option_text: Notify the Board only after the next inspection.
options.original_rationale: The notice deadline is independent of an inspection.
options.independent_option_analysis: Next inspection is not the notice trigger.

options.option_text: Notify only the pharmacy's home-state regulator.
options.original_rationale: The Massachusetts Board must be notified of the change.
options.independent_option_analysis: Home-state notice alone does not replace MA Board notice.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts hospital pharmacy proposes keeping its Schedule II morphine stock in an unlocked automated room because the system has a digital audit trail. Under DPH hospital accountability guidelines, which control remains necessary?
questions.author_citation: MA DPH General Accountability Guidelines, Pharmacy Department: Schedule II

options.option_text: A digital log eliminates the need to secure bulk Schedule II stock.
options.original_rationale: An electronic audit trail does not replace physical access controls.

options.option_text: Any licensed hospital employee may access bulk Schedule II stock without pharmacist oversight.
options.original_rationale: Hospital pharmacy vault access is restricted to licensed pharmacists under the guideline.

options.option_text: Store bulk Schedule II drugs in a restricted pharmacist-access vault with perpetual records.
options.original_rationale: The DPH hospital/clinic guideline specifically addresses physical Schedule II security and hard-copy perpetual accountability.

options.option_text: Periodic refill counts alone replace Schedule II perpetual tracking.
options.original_rationale: The guideline requires perpetual accounting for these drugs.

questions.question_stem: At a Massachusetts hospital pharmacy, bulk Schedule III and IV tablets are proposed to be mixed in one unlabeled picking bin with noncontrolled medications. The pharmacist says weekly purchase totals are sufficient. What should change?
questions.author_citation: MA DPH General Accountability Guidelines, Pharmacy Department: Schedule III–IV

options.option_text: Allow mixing because Schedule III–IV medicines may be stored like Schedule VI in this setting.
options.original_rationale: The DPH hospital guidance specifically disallows commingling of pharmacy bulk Schedule III–IV stock.

options.option_text: Keep the mixed bin but sign a monthly attestation.
options.original_rationale: An attestation does not replace required separation and inventory controls.

options.option_text: Permit unrestricted access to bulk Schedule III–IV stock by any hospital employee.
options.original_rationale: The guidance limits bulk Schedule III–IV access to licensed pharmacists.

options.option_text: Separate and secure the bulk Schedule III–IV inventory and maintain perpetual accountability.
options.original_rationale: This applies the hospital-specific noncommingling, access and inventory requirements.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts hospital stores a refrigerated Schedule II injection in a regular unlocked nursing refrigerator shared with patient snacks. The hospital uses barcoded administration records. Which required protection is missing?
questions.author_citation: DPH General Accountability Guidelines, Nursing Units: Refrigerated Controlled Substances

options.option_text: Use a double-locked refrigerator dedicated to controlled nursing-unit medication.
options.original_rationale: DPH's hospital and clinic accountability guidelines expressly call for double-locked refrigerated controlled-stock storage.

options.option_text: A barcode record is sufficient even if any unit visitor can open the refrigerator.
options.original_rationale: Electronic tracing does not waive physical security controls for Schedule II–V stock.

options.option_text: Move the drug to the hospital cafeteria's locked food freezer.
options.original_rationale: Medication storage must be secure and maintain the manufacturer's specified temperature.

options.option_text: Store all controlled refrigerated medication at ambient temperature until medication administration.
options.original_rationale: Cold-chain requirements remain applicable to refrigerated controlled drugs.

questions.question_stem: A hospital nurse gives part of an ordered Schedule II injection and must discard the unused remainder. Two licensed staff are available; a supervisor suggests that a single unlicensed orderly may document the waste. What is appropriate?
questions.author_citation: MA DPH General Accountability Guidelines, Nursing Units: Schedule II–V

options.option_text: Two licensed staff must witness and co-sign the partial-dose disposal.
options.original_rationale: The DPH guideline specifies two licensed staff and appropriate signed documentation for unused Schedule II–V portions.

options.option_text: Have the orderly alone discard it as ordinary trash.
options.original_rationale: An unlicensed orderly cannot substitute for the designated licensed witness/waste process.

options.option_text: Enter the unused remainder as an intact, never-administered pharmacy return.
options.original_rationale: A partial dose remaining after patient administration is not an intact returned unit.

options.option_text: Wait for a pharmacy technician to remove the cabinet from service indefinitely.
options.original_rationale: The guideline provides a documented, witnessed wasting route rather than an indefinite hold.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist proposes being Manager of Record of TWO unrelated retail pharmacies, averaging 12 working hours per week at each. Both owners agree. What is the state practice limitation?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 247 CMR 9.23(3)-(4) MOR hours and one-retail-pharmacy restriction

options.option_text: Two MOR positions are permitted if a single technician is physically stationed in both pharmacies.
options.original_rationale: The MOR role is personal and cannot be transferred to a technician.
options.independent_option_analysis: A technician cannot replace MOR personal role.

options.option_text: The pharmacist may count remote conference calls as the full weekly physical-presence requirement.
options.original_rationale: The regulation specifies an average weekly working-hours obligation as MOR.
options.independent_option_analysis: Remote calls alone do not satisfy the described MOR onsite working-time condition.

options.option_text: Corporate consent alone removes MOR practice-hour and one-retail-pharmacy limits.
options.original_rationale: Owner consent does not supersede 247 CMR 9.23.
options.independent_option_analysis: Owner approval does not waive regulatory restrictions.

options.option_text: The MOR must average at least 30 weekly hours and manage only one retail pharmacy at a time.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 9.23(3)–(4) sets these limits, subject to the regulation's applicability and exceptions.
options.independent_option_analysis: At least 30 weekly hours on average and only one retail pharmacy MOR, under stated ordinary scenario.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy's permanent Manager of Record resigns and the Board is not informed because the owners assume that appointing a temporary shift pharmacist is sufficient. Which separate state deadline applies?
questions.preexisting_legal_hold: Overlap of MOR 10-day individual notice and 14-day pharmacy reporting needs final legal review.
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 247 CMR 20.05(1) pharmacy MOR-change report 14 calendar days; distinct individual deadline conflict 9.23(2)(f)/20.05(3)
questions.scope_or_source_caveat: Correct as narrowly worded about pharmacy only; MOR-individual 10-day versus 14-calendar-day text conflict remains unresolved.

options.option_text: Report the MOR change to the Board within 14 calendar days of the change.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 20.05(1) sets the resident pharmacy's Board-notice deadline.
options.independent_option_analysis: Pharmacy must notify Board within 14 calendar days.

options.option_text: Notify only the Medicare contractor within 30 days.
options.original_rationale: The Massachusetts Board has its own professional registration notification process.
options.independent_option_analysis: Medicare-only notice cannot substitute for Board notice.

options.option_text: No notice is needed if a pharmacist is always on duty.
options.original_rationale: Pharmacist coverage does not replace MOR-specific Board reporting.
options.independent_option_analysis: Ordinary shift pharmacist coverage does not cancel MOR notice requirement.

options.option_text: Wait until the next renewal date and report the former MOR's resignation then.
options.original_rationale: The state regulation imposes a shorter notice clock.
options.independent_option_analysis: Renewal delay violates earlier pharmacy duty.

questions.question_stem: Flooding forces a Massachusetts retail pharmacy to stop all ordinary pharmacy services. The suspension will exceed 24 hours, but the owner assumes the business may simply resume when repaired with no regulatory communication. Which distinct action is required?

options.option_text: Report only after 100 days of closure.
options.original_rationale: The >24-hour interruption has a separate notification rule.

options.option_text: Replace the pharmacy's DEA registration automatically because every power interruption changes legal ownership.
options.original_rationale: A power disruption does not by itself establish ownership change.

options.option_text: Notify the Board as required for a suspension of pharmacy operations exceeding 24 hours.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 9.19(15) requires notification of an extended interruption of operations.

options.option_text: Destroy all patient profiles when the facility reopens.
options.original_rationale: Legal record retention and continuity-of-care duties remain.

questions.question_stem: A pharmacy cites proposed 2026 amendments to 105 CMR 700.000 at an October public hearing and insists the proposal immediately overrides still-operative 247 CMR pharmacy controls. What is the best legal review?
questions.author_citation: DPH 105 CMR 700.000 proposed amendments public hearing Oct 19, 2026; current 247 CMR 9.00

options.option_text: Every published proposal is binding upon public hearing announcement.
options.original_rationale: A proposal does not become operative merely by holding a hearing.

options.option_text: Apply current regulations and check whether the proposal became effective.
options.original_rationale: As of the November 20 review, the official DPH page describes amendments as proposed, not in force.

options.option_text: Ignore all 105 CMR rules because Board regulations have priority.
options.original_rationale: Both legally effective DPH and Board rules may apply within their jurisdictions.

options.option_text: Apply the proposed text retrospectively to all existing pharmacy records.
options.original_rationale: Neither the described proposal nor retroactivity is established.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts retail drug store holds an ordinary Drug Store Pharmacy license. Management plans to begin compounding STERILE preparations on-site, but the owner says its regular drug store license alone is sufficient. Which license combination is required?

options.option_text: The Drug Store Pharmacy license alone is enough if a pharmacist has completed sterile compounding CE.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 6.02(2) requires an additional sterile compounding pharmacy license for retail sterile compounding.

options.option_text: An ordinary Drug Store Pharmacy license plus a sterile compounding pharmacy license.
options.original_rationale: The rule lists this combination unless the facility qualifies under the distinct institutional sterile compounding route.

options.option_text: A manufacturer wholesaler license alone, because sterile CSPs are always mass-manufactured products.
options.original_rationale: Retail pharmacy compounding is not automatically exempted from Board licensing through wholesaling.

options.option_text: A single pharmacy technician certificate, without a facility license change.
options.original_rationale: Individual staff certification is not the pharmacy authorization.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts-licensed NONRESIDENT retail pharmacy located in another state plans to cease all operations. It wants to notify Massachusetts only after its final fill. Which Massachusetts Board notice requirement is correct?

options.option_text: No state notice is ever required because the premises are outside Massachusetts.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 6.13(2) expressly covers nonresident pharmacies.

options.option_text: Only notify the DEA and patients, not the Massachusetts Board.
options.original_rationale: Nonresident pharmacy closure has a separate Board notice.

options.option_text: Notify the Board by certified mail at least 14 days before closing.
options.original_rationale: The nonresident closure subsection specifies the notice and basic pharmacy-identifying information.

options.option_text: Mail the Board notice 90 days after closing.
options.original_rationale: The statutory period is an advance notice, not a postclosure deadline.

questions.question_stem: An out-of-state retail pharmacy wants to dispense patient-specific COMPLEX NONSTERILE compounded preparations by mail into Massachusetts. The facility has a home-state pharmacy permit and a Massachusetts NONRESIDENT Drug Store Pharmacy license, but no Massachusetts nonresident complex nonsterile license. What is still required?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 247 CMR 6.02(6) nonresident complex nonsterile compounded drug shipment

options.option_text: Only proof of the pharmacist's U.S. citizenship.
options.original_rationale: The state licensing prerequisite concerns the facility and its compounded products.
options.independent_option_analysis: License test concerns facility authorizations, not pharmacist citizenship.

options.option_text: A new Massachusetts 503B outsourcing registration for ordinary patient-specific 503A dispensing.
options.original_rationale: The facility is described as a pharmacy dispensing to specific patients, not a §503B outsourcing facility.
options.independent_option_analysis: Patient-specific 503A scenario does not automatically require 503B registration.

options.option_text: No additional license because the drug is dispensed from another state.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 6.02(6) expressly regulates shipments of complex nonsterile CSPs into the Commonwealth.
options.independent_option_analysis: Nonresident location does not remove MA licensing obligations.

options.option_text: The separate nonresident complex nonsterile compounding pharmacy license.
options.original_rationale: The regulation requires it in addition to the nonresident Drug Store Pharmacy license.
options.independent_option_analysis: Separate nonresident complex nonsterile license required in addition to Drug Store Pharmacy license.

questions.question_stem: Two Massachusetts-licensed pharmacies lawfully transfer their remaining controlled-stock inventory during a closure after giving the Board the required advance notice. Both Managers of Record signed the transfer inventory. What post-transfer filing is required?

options.option_text: Only file DEA Form 222 for all Schedule VI drugs; no state attestation applies.
options.original_rationale: DEA Form 222 does not replace the state Board's inventory attestation.

options.option_text: Send a quarterly inventory aggregate to the FDA instead of the Board.
options.original_rationale: The regulation requires specific post-transfer confirmation to the Board.

options.option_text: Both pharmacies file a controlled-inventory attestation with the Board within ten days.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 6.14(2)(d) establishes this requirement.

options.option_text: The transferor pharmacy may keep controlled stock for months after transfer as a backup.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 6.14(2)(f) prohibits the transferor from retaining controlled substances after transfer.

questions.question_stem: A licensed out-of-state pharmacy dispenses prescriptions to Massachusetts residents by mail. Its compliance director argues that Massachusetts law applies only to pharmacy buildings physically inside Massachusetts. What is correct?

options.option_text: The pharmacy may ignore Massachusetts dispensing rules if its home state pharmacy permit remains active.
options.original_rationale: The Massachusetts nonresident licensing framework imposes state dispensing and shipping duties.

options.option_text: Follow applicable Massachusetts dispensing and shipment laws, including their nonresident exceptions.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 9.20 specifies this nonresident practice standard.

options.option_text: Every subsection of 247 CMR 9.19 applies with no exceptions.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 9.19(23) expressly exempts certain operational provisions for nonresident pharmacies.

options.option_text: Only the federal DEA rules apply to any interstate shipment.
options.original_rationale: Federal requirements coexist with applicable Massachusetts state rules.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts-located registered 503B outsourcing facility plans to change legal ownership in 45 days. The registrant assumes the usual 14-day retail-pharmacy ownership notice applies to all compounding facilities. What special requirement applies?

options.option_text: Notify the Board at least 60 days before the outsourcing-facility ownership transfer.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 21.08(2) imposes this advance notice on Massachusetts-located outsourcing facilities.

options.option_text: Notify the Board only after the new owner ships its first sterile CSP.
options.original_rationale: The state regulation imposes advance notice and prohibits dispensing before authorization.

options.option_text: No Board notice if FDA has an active 503B listing.
options.original_rationale: The federal listing does not waive state ownership reporting.

options.option_text: Use the pharmacy intern's personal license as the facility license during the ownership transition.
options.original_rationale: An individual license does not substitute for facility registration.

questions.question_stem: A proposed Massachusetts 503B outsourcing facility has a current FDA Section 503B registration but has no evidence of an FDA inspection during the two years immediately before its Massachusetts application. Under 247 CMR 21.02, what is missing?

options.option_text: Proof of an FDA inspection during the two years before the Massachusetts application.
options.original_rationale: The Massachusetts application expressly requires inspection evidence within the prior two years.

options.option_text: Only proof that its supervising physician holds a DEA number.
options.original_rationale: A physician's DEA registration does not replace the facility's FDA inspection documentation.

options.option_text: A 15-year-old certificate from any voluntary quality association.
options.original_rationale: The regulation specifies an FDA inspection and recency.

options.option_text: Nothing; FDA registration alone supplies all required Massachusetts documents.
options.original_rationale: The Board additionally lists inspection and other requirements.

questions.question_stem: An appropriately registered Massachusetts outsourcing facility receives FDA Form 483 inspection observations but has no immediate disciplinary order. Management asks whether reporting to the Massachusetts Board may wait until the facility's next registration renewal. What is required?

options.option_text: Wait for an FDA Warning Letter, because Form 483 is never a state notification event.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 21.09 specifically names receipt of FDA Form 483 independently of a warning letter.

options.option_text: Notify the Board in writing within 14 days of receipt of the FDA Form 483.
options.original_rationale: The outsourcing notification regulation has a 14-day reporting duty.

options.option_text: Report only if more than five percent of the facility's stockholders change.
options.original_rationale: Ownership-change notice is a distinct trigger from inspection observations.

options.option_text: Mail the report only to DEA because inspection findings are controlled-substance information.
options.original_rationale: FDA quality observations are subject to Board notification under 247 CMR 21.09.

questions.question_stem: A HIPAA-covered Massachusetts pharmacy discovers a reportable breach of unsecured PHI affecting 34 patients in October 2026. No exception or law-enforcement delay applies. Which federal reporting timetable is correct?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 45 CFR 164.404(b) individual notice without unreasonable delay max 60 days, 164.408(c) small-breach HHS year-end+60

options.option_text: Notify affected patients only with the next annual HIPAA report.
options.original_rationale: Affected individuals have a prompt, no-later-than-60-day notification rule.
options.independent_option_analysis: Patient notification cannot wait for annual HHS filing.

options.option_text: Notify patients within 60 days; report to HHS by 60 days after year-end.
options.original_rationale: HIPAA has separate individual and small-breach HHS reporting clocks.
options.independent_option_analysis: Separate deadlines: individuals max 60 days; HHS under-500 within 60 days after year-end.

options.option_text: Notify both HHS and each patient only after the calendar year closes.
options.original_rationale: The HHS under-500 schedule does not defer individual notice.
options.independent_option_analysis: Year-end HHS rule does not delay individual notice.

options.option_text: HIPAA never applies when fewer than 500 people are affected.
options.original_rationale: Small breaches still require notification.
options.independent_option_analysis: Under-500 breaches remain notifiable.

questions.question_stem: A covered pharmacy determines that a breach of unsecured PHI has affected 520 people. The risk assessment did not establish a low probability of compromise and no permitted delay applies. Which HHS notification standard governs?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 45 CFR 164.408(b), 164.404(b): >=500 HHS notice contemporaneous with individual notice, without unreasonable delay max 60 days

options.option_text: Only the next annual small-breach log.
options.original_rationale: That option applies to fewer than 500 affected individuals.
options.independent_option_analysis: Annual small-breach log applies to fewer than 500.

options.option_text: An open-ended deadline decided by the pharmacy's vendor.
options.original_rationale: Business arrangements do not eliminate the regulated timing.
options.independent_option_analysis: Vendor discretion does not suspend federal notification time.

options.option_text: Notice solely to Massachusetts police; HHS is never involved.
options.original_rationale: A covered entity must follow the federal HHS breach-reporting rule.
options.independent_option_analysis: HHS notification is a federal duty, not replaced by state police-only notice.

options.option_text: Notify HHS without unreasonable delay, within 60 calendar days.
options.original_rationale: The at-least-500 category requires timely reporting to the HHS Secretary.
options.independent_option_analysis: Report to HHS without unreasonable delay within individual notice max-60-day clock.

questions.question_stem: A HIPAA-covered pharmacy discovers a reportable breach of unsecured PHI involving 25 patients. Twelve affected patients have outdated mailing addresses and no current email addresses. What substitute notification route may be required for these hard-to-reach individuals?
questions.author_citation: 45 CFR 164.404(d)(2); HHS HIPAA Breach Notification Rule

options.option_text: No notice is needed because their original mailing information is outdated.
options.original_rationale: A lack of current contact information does not eliminate notification requirements.

options.option_text: Use a 90-day website notice or major-media notice, with a toll-free contact number.
options.original_rationale: HIPAA substitute notice rule provides these options when contact information is insufficient for ten or more people.

options.option_text: Keep a confidential staff-only memo with no public notice.
options.original_rationale: An internal memorandum does not reach affected individuals.

options.option_text: Send the pharmacy's standard payment invoice to one representative of the group.
options.original_rationale: A payment invoice to an unrelated person is not an authorized substitute notice.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy discovers that an unauthorized person obtained a file containing Massachusetts residents' personal information as defined under M.G.L. c.93H. A supervisor assumes the HIPAA 60-day outside limit authorizes waiting 60 days for ALL Massachusetts notices. Which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

options.option_text: Massachusetts Chapter 93H notification duties have their own 'as soon as practicable and without unreasonable delay' standard.
options.original_rationale: The state breach statute has its own timeliness rule.

options.option_text: If HIPAA applies, complying with its outer deadline automatically satisfies every state's notice requirement.
options.original_rationale: Federal and state notification clocks and covered data can differ.

options.option_text: The organization must consider its written information security program and applicable state reporting duties.
options.original_rationale: 201 CMR 17.00 requires a comprehensive WISP for qualifying personal information and state reporting rules apply.

options.option_text: Massachusetts law exempts healthcare organizations from all WISP safeguards.
options.original_rationale: Healthcare entities are not categorically exempt from the Massachusetts safeguards.

questions.question_stem: Two Massachusetts retail pharmacies share prescription processing. A drug interaction alert was overridden remotely, and the software records only a generic 'completed' status with no user identity or time. Which improvement is required under Board shared-service policy?

options.option_text: Log processing steps, the responsible people and the dates/times.
options.original_rationale: Board Policy 2021-02 requires an audit trail including date/time and the individuals involved.

options.option_text: Delete the remote event because the final pharmacist reviewed the label.
options.original_rationale: Final review does not remove the audit-trail obligation.

options.option_text: Share only a weekly total of all prescriptions without case detail.
options.original_rationale: An aggregate volume report cannot trace a single questionable transaction.

options.option_text: Allow anyone at either pharmacy to use the same generic login.
options.original_rationale: An unaccountable shared login undermines required traceability and data integrity.

questions.question_stem: Two independently owned Massachusetts pharmacies plan a remote processing relationship. They do not share an owner and have no written service agreement, but both use the same computer software. What does the Board policy require?

options.option_text: Common software alone is a complete substitute for written responsibilities.
options.original_rationale: Technical access does not satisfy the written agreement requirement for independent owners.

options.option_text: Write a shared-service agreement assigning each pharmacy's duties and oversight.
options.original_rationale: The policy allows shared service among different owners when a suitable written contract exists.

options.option_text: Buy an additional DEA Form 222 for each remotely reviewed Schedule VI prescription.
options.original_rationale: A Form 222 is a Schedule II order instrument, not a shared-service contract.

options.option_text: Stop all processing even after a compliant written agreement exists.
options.original_rationale: The policy permits qualifying shared services.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy has operated under a valid written central-fill shared-service agreement for three years. Its staff review policies only when an adverse event occurs and have not documented an annual review. What must change?

options.option_text: The written agreement automatically removes all policy review obligations once signed.
options.original_rationale: Board shared-service policy requires ongoing compliance review of procedures.

options.option_text: A biennial review is sufficient if both pharmacies have the same software.
options.original_rationale: Use of shared software does not determine the required policy-review frequency.

options.option_text: Review shared-service policies and procedures at least annually and document needed updates.
options.original_rationale: Board Policy 2021-02 §III(n)–(o) requires participating pharmacies to maintain and review procedures.

options.option_text: Only the remote pharmacy has documentation duties; the originating pharmacy is fully exempt.
options.original_rationale: Participating pharmacies share defined responsibilities and required procedures.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts originating pharmacy learns that its participating central-fill location had an electronic record outage and cannot produce a reliable patient-specific audit trail for a prepared medication. The originating store wants to release the package solely because its shipping label matches. What should occur?

options.option_text: Release automatically because central-fill work is wholly the other store's responsibility.
options.original_rationale: Participants are jointly accountable and patient safety may not be compromised.

options.option_text: Erase the outage from the shared database to restore the planned transaction history.
options.original_rationale: Deletion defeats secure record integrity and traceability.

options.option_text: Hand the package to the courier without final validation.
options.original_rationale: Final dispensing validation and applicable shared-service controls still apply.

options.option_text: Hold release until the patient-specific record is verified and the responsible parties identified.
options.original_rationale: The joint controls require a valid, auditable prescription process.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy dispenses a manufacturer's refrigerated injection that must remain at 2–8°C. An outsourced courier says temperature control only matters while the injection is physically inside the pharmacy. Which rule addresses the shipment?

options.option_text: Maintain the required cold chain during transportation and delivery too.
options.original_rationale: Board Policy 2020-05 §II explicitly applies cold-chain control to delivery and shipping.

options.option_text: Move the injection to an ambient shipping bag once it leaves the building.
options.original_rationale: The manufacturer's specified stability and the cold chain continue during transit.

options.option_text: Change the package label to 'room temperature' without stability evidence.
options.original_rationale: Relabeling cannot override storage specifications.
